candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: The freedom grounding moral responsibility is compatible with determinism, while libertarian or indeterminist freedom is an expendable fantasy.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted turn follows the explicit handoff to Dennett and consistently presents his compatibilist position in the first person.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly defines the compatibilist side of the motion and distinguishes responsibility-preserving freedom from the libertarian conception both speakers reject.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's published characterization of Dennett's compatibilism as mistaken or quasi-theological.

candidates.contextSummary: After discussing their contentious written exchange, Dennett argues that Harris already accepts determinism-compatible responsibility and is therefore close to compatibilism.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Ordinary free agency consists in the competence to undertake obligations and act responsibly, capacities that depend on a functioning nervous system rather than indeterminism.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett continues the same uninterrupted turn, using first-person examples and explicitly identifying the sense of free will he considers important.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move supplies concrete criteria for the compatibilist freedom at issue and explains why some agents possess it while impaired agents may not.
candidates.contextSummary: Dennett moves from broad agreement about naturalism to contracts, promises, disability, and nervous-system competence as practical markers of responsible agency.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Compatibilism legitimately preserves a naturalistic concept of free will by discarding inherited magical commitments rather than accepting traditional usage as decisive.
candidates.attributionBasis: The passage begins with Dennett explicitly stating his view of compatibilism and remains his sustained answer until Harris begins responding in the final row.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This explains the conceptual method behind Dennett's position and answers the charge that revising free will amounts to theology or doctrinal evasion.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's request for Dennett to state compatibilism and address Harris's earlier theological characterization.

candidates.contextSummary: Asked to define compatibilism, Dennett compares free will with consciousness and argues that naturalistic conceptual revision can preserve a real phenomenon without its magical interpretation.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Compatibilism risks changing the subject when it removes features that are integral to the concept people mean by free will rather than merely correcting incidental folk beliefs.
candidates.attributionBasis: Harris audibly takes over during the opening source row and frames the ensuing first-person objection as his established gripe with compatibilism.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The objection targets whether compatibilist freedom answers the original free-will problem at all, making it a direct challenge to the opposing side's central definition.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's claim that free will can be retained after its mysterious or magical interpretation is discarded.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris accepts that concepts can be purified but distinguishes legitimate explanation from eliminating core features and then applying the original label to a different phenomenon.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Freedom is the controlled possession of many practical degrees of action, especially the sophisticated capacity to be moved by reasons, not exemption from determinism.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett explicitly introduces a new line of argument and develops it continuously through engineering, control theory, and reasons-responsive competence.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move offers Dennett's positive core account of free will and places reasons-responsive control, rather than causal indeterminacy, at the center of the motion.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's contention that compatibilism changes the subject by eliminating the concept's allegedly ineliminable core.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett rejects a sharp boundary between clarification and subject change, then uses engineering degrees of freedom to explain the distinctive versatility and control of human agents.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Responsible agency is a graded package of beliefs, ordered desires, attention, reasons-responsiveness, and self-control whose presence distinguishes free from unfree agents regardless of determinism.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett continues his uninterrupted explanation, poses a question about ideal responsibility, and supplies a detailed answer in his own theoretical vocabulary.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This operationalizes reasons-responsive freedom, identifies how it can be impaired or usurped, and connects the resulting classification directly to moral responsibility.
candidates.contextSummary: Using a defective chess program and the model of a trustworthy adult, Dennett argues that freedom depends on available capacities and their control, not on the causal structure of the universe.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Compatibilism neglects the first-person authorship and ability-to-do-otherwise experience that motivates the free-will problem, replacing the mythical object of concern with an agreed but different reality.
candidates.attributionBasis: Harris begins by qualifying his agreement with Dennett and then speaks continuously through his phenomenological account and extended Atlantis analogy.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move states Harris's principal case against compatibilism: its useful capacities do not answer the subjective libertarian claim whose falsity makes free will problematic.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's reasons-responsive account of responsible agency and claim that determinism is irrelevant to distinguishing free and unfree agents.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris contrasts third-person capacities with the felt authorship of thoughts and choices, denies that an identical rewind permits another action, and likens compatibilist preservation to renaming Sicily as Atlantis.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Naturalistic freedom preserves the responsibility-relevant distinctions people need, and deliberating agents require an actionable sense of open alternatives without requiring magical or exact-replay alternatives.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett acknowledges Harris's analogy and then gives a sustained first-person response covering responsibility, deliberation, nearby alternatives, and a deterministic chess example.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly answers Harris's phenomenological objection by explaining both why nonmagical freedom matters and how meaningful alternative possibilities function within deterministic agency.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's claim that people's real concern is libertarian authorship and that compatibilism substitutes a different phenomenon.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett concedes that magical freedom does not exist but argues that agents must treat some matters as open, and that nearby-world variation can justify saying an agent could have acted otherwise.

candidates.speaker: Sam Harris
candidates.proposition: Even tiny physical contingencies governing major choices undermine the ordinary felt picture of autonomous personhood by revealing the agent as dependent on causal factors outside conscious authorship.
candidates.attributionBasis: Harris explicitly agrees before marking what Dennett has not acknowledged, then develops the first-person challenge through examples involving marriage and life-changing decisions.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move presses the psychological and metaphysical consequence Harris thinks remains after accepting Dennett's nearby-alternatives account: conscious agency still lacks ultimate authorship.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's deterministic chess example and claim that small nearby changes justify saying an agent could have done otherwise.

candidates.contextSummary: Harris argues that a synaptic charge or similarly minute condition could redirect an entire life, reviving the image of marionette strings even though no external puppeteer exists.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Absolute indeterminacy would not create free will, while reasons-responsive determination can support responsibility because different choices require changes proportionate to the balance of reasons.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett clearly takes the microphone, labels Harris partly right and partly wrong, and maintains the floor through the delivered boundary context.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The response rejects indeterminacy as a solution and begins a positive account linking responsible choice to deliberative reasons and robust determination rather than causal randomness.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Harris's argument that sensitivity to tiny physical differences restores marionette strings and subverts ordinary personhood.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett distinguishes genuine toss-ups from decisions where reasons strongly favor one side, then invokes the libertarian demand for an undetermined choice and Luther's responsible declaration that he could do no other.
